title: Deep-Layer Attention Pruning for Vision-Language Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to prune visual tokens for efficient vision-language model (VLM) inference on spatially-sensitive tasks without requiring offline calibration. Several prior papers address visual token pruning for efficient VLM inference, but none explicitly focus on spatially-sensitive tasks without offline calibration. For example, [1], [2], [3], [5], and [6] all discuss token pruning for efficiency, but they do not explicitly target spatial sensitivity or the absence of offline calibration. [9] mentions attention debiasing but does not address spatial sensitivity as a primary objective. Therefore, no prior paper fully matches the purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves extracting text-to-vision attention from a deeper LLM layer (layer 12 of 32 in InternVL2.5-8B) and applying Maximal Independent Set (MIS) selection directly without debiasing. MIS selection is a well-known graph-theoretic approach, and [25] discusses the statistical mechanics of maximal independent sets, while [18] and [28] discuss submodular optimization and pruning methods that could be related. However, none of these papers apply MIS directly to text-to-vision attention in VLMs, nor do they describe the specific combination of deeper-layer attention extraction and MIS selection without debiasing. Thus, the mechanism is not covered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg benchmarks and grounding accuracy as the metric, comparing performance against D2Pruner. RefCOCO and its variants are standard benchmarks for visual grounding tasks, and grounding accuracy is a widely used metric in this domain. For example, [1], [2], [5], and [6] all use similar benchmarks and metrics for evaluating token pruning methods. While the specific comparison to D2Pruner is new, the evaluation design (benchmark family and metric semantics) is not novel. Therefore, the evaluation is covered.

### Domain
The domain is vision-language model inference efficiency, specifically focusing on visual token pruning for grounding tasks. This domain is well-established in prior work, as evidenced by [1], [2], [3], [5], and [6], which all address visual token pruning for efficient VLM inference. While the specific focus on spatially-sensitive tasks is new, this is a sub-problem within the broader domain of VLM inference efficiency. Thus, the domain is covered.

Both papers use standard evaluation designs (accuracy comparison against baselines) that match the contribution's evaluation design. Therefore, the evaluation is **covered** by [8] and [17].

Papers [1], [2], [5], [6], [8], and [11] all address visual token pruning in vision-language models, including applications to grounding tasks. ### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to explain why prior ratio-based debiasing is unnecessary and harmful. Paper [4] discusses attention debiasing for token pruning in vision-language models, identifying systematic biases in attention mechanisms and their impact on pruning. While [4] focuses on positional bias correction, it does not explicitly address the harm caused by ratio-based debiasing methods or refute their necessity. Paper [6] analyzes position bias in transformers but does not critique ratio-based debiasing methods. No prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship or directly refutes the necessity of ratio-based debiasing.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses a phase-0 diagnostic analysis measuring Spearman correlation between attention and token position across layers, combined with an ablation applying the ratio formula \(A_{\text{mid}} / (A_{\text{shallow}} + \epsilon)\) at multiple layers. Paper [6] provides a graph-theoretic framework for analyzing position bias in multi-layer attention, which overlaps conceptually with measuring correlations between attention and position. However, [6] does not use Spearman correlation or the specific ratio formula applied across layers. Paper [4] discusses positional bias correction but does not employ the same diagnostic or ablation methods. No prior paper uses the exact mechanism described.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring position correlation (Spearman rho values) and assessing the degradation in accuracy caused by ratio debiasing. Paper [6] quantifies positional bias using graph-theoretic metrics, which is a different evaluation design. Paper [4] evaluates positional bias correction methods but does not use Spearman correlation or assess accuracy degradation due to ratio debiasing. Paper [10] evaluates debiasing methods in image classification but does not use the same metrics or validation framework. No prior paper matches the evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of vision-language model inference efficiency, specifically visual token pruning for grounding. Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], and [7] all address token pruning or efficiency improvements in vision-language models, making the domain covered. While the specific sub-problem (refuting ratio-based debiasing) is new, the general application area is not.
